title: The thousandth morning
hookLine: a thousand days of a few minutes each: the long story you've joined

lines: AMEN. LET THERE BE LIGHT. I WILL NOT FAIL YOU.
A FEW MINUTES AT A TIME.
cards: The first word on this path was amen: let it be so. Then came the stories, the practices, the long reading of the text. A second year opened with in the beginning, and let there be light.
A third opened with a promise: I will not fail you. In between, mornings. Some on a bus.
Some at a kitchen table before anyone else was up. Some missed or rested, and then a fresh start. A few minutes each.
Stacked up, they reach a number worth stopping for.

teach.b: The Bible uses the word thousand in a few surprising places, and none of them is a scoreboard.
Psalm 90 carries the heading "A Prayer of Moses the man of God", and it says to God: "For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night."
A thousand years, to God, is one night shift.

teach.h: ONE DAY AS A THOUSAND YEARS.
teach.b: The second letter of Peter echoes that line and turns it both ways: "one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day."
So a single morning can carry real weight, and a thousand of them are small in God's hands. Both at once.
Psalm 84 weighs it differently again: "For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand." Then Lamentations, a book of grief over a fallen city.
In the middle of its grief: "They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." That's the hinge. In these lines the faithfulness belongs to God, not to the count.
The morning is new whether yesterday went well or not.
A monk chanting the same psalms at dawn, a grandmother saying the same prayer at the kitchen sink, a commuter with headphones on a train: each is building a life out of small, repeated mornings.
The long story this year has told was carried that way. Not by big moments alone, but by people who did one small faithful thing, and then did it again.

how: Some Christians keep a short daily time of prayer or reading, often in the morning, and some pray set psalms at fixed hours, as monks and nuns do, returning to the same words day after day.

o: a book of the prophets' complaints against kings
a Bible book of grief over a fallen city
a set of sad hymns sung at Christian funerals

games.q: a thousand, the Bible's way — tap the pairs.
p: a thousand years in thy sight
as yesterday when it is past

s: in Psalm 90, a thousand years in God's sight are like yesterday
"as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night."
2 Peter only says a thousand years are as one day
it runs both ways: "one day is with the Lord as a thousand years" as well.
Lamentations says God's mercies are new every year
every morning: "they are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness."

games.q: the psalmist weighs one day near God against a thousand days anywhere else. which does Psalm 84 choose?
o: the thousand days; more is more.
the one day in God's courts.
neither; all days weigh the same.
games.why: Psalm 84:10: "for a day in thy courts is better than a thousand." the psalm would rather be a doorkeeper in God's house than live anywhere else.

practice: Let a few mornings from this path come back on their own, a word that stuck, a story, the place you were sitting when you heard it, without grading them.
Then let one thank-you rise, for a person, a line, or the plain fact of having come back.
If you pray, you can give thanks in your own words or the psalm's, a day in thy courts is better than a thousand; if you don't, just let the thanks be there.

wordCard.voice: Lamentations. The book of grief that still says mercies are new every morning, the hinge this lesson turns on after a thousand days of small practice.

orig.note: Hebrew: a thousand — the word in Psalm 90:4, a thousand years in thy sight.

carryVoice: Your line: a thousand mornings. Each one new. That's day one thousand.
